parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child, a brat
an air is a look or manner someone has

explanation.surface: A child undermines authority with a cheeky look.
explanation.definitionFit: To weaken or damage something gradually is to undermine it.

clue.text: Routine procedure where baby awaits birth

indicators.note: procedure hints that the letters of routine go through a process that reorders them

explanation.surface: A standard hospital procedure for an expectant mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'procedure' rearranges ROUTINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for inside the womb, describing the unborn child before delivery.

indicators.note: cut means the boy's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Patrick is a typical Irish man's name, after the patron saint
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A noble from Ireland is snubbed by a man from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' docks the K from PATRICK; 'by' is a link before IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome the noble class were the patricians, so the word means of high birth, aristocratic.

clue.text: Competitors need to enter for these games

definitions.text: Competitors need to enter for these games

parts.words: Competitors need to enter for these games
parts.note: entering a competition is reread as walking through an entrance into a building

explanation.surface: Athletes must sign up before taking part in these events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enter' means sign up for a contest on the surface; cryptically it means going in through a door.
explanation.definitionFit: Games played inside a building rather than outdoors, like darts or table tennis.

clue.text: Show party promises to be endless

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the party's programme is dropped

parts.note: a manifesto is the set of promises a political party publishes

explanation.surface: A party's pledges are meant to go on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link; 'endless' cuts the last letter off MANIFESTO.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to make plain or display something is to show it.

clue.text: Old indian currency goes up and down

indicators.note: goes up and down means the word reads the same up or down the grid

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A former coin's value fluctuates.
explanation.walkthrough: In a Down entry, the word reads the same from top or bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A former coin of British India, worth one sixteenth of a rupee.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'A boisterous foreign port (8)': no parse of these words gives ISTANBUL (no anagram fodder of eight letters fits), so the clue looks garbled by OCR and no source gives the printed text.

clue.text: Nun that is upset by lack of interest

indicators.note: upset means the letters are knocked over and rearranged

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A nun is troubled by everyone's indifference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges NUN plus IE; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Boredom and listlessness, a weariness with everything, is a lack of interest.

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of breadth are arranged in an odd new way

explanation.surface: A comment on the remarkable range of Shakespeare's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges all seven letters of BREADTH; 'The' and 'of' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare is known by the epithet referring to him as the poet of Avon.

indicators.note: removed suggests the letters of in duty are shifted out of their places and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is careless while on duty, and gets taken off it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removed' rearranges the six letters of IN DUTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloppy work is messy and careless, lacking neatness.

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a stance is a position or viewpoint on an issue

explanation.surface: A viewpoint held by many, given as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works through the phrase 'for instance', which means the same as 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: An illustrative case cited to make a point serves as an example.

indicators.note: incorrect means the letters of in angle are set out wrongly, rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is set at the wrong angle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incorrect' rearranges IN ANGLE, and the whole clue also describes something tilted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tilting off the vertical is set at an incorrect angle.

parts.note: instalments suggests hire-purchase payments on a television set, but means the parts of a serial shown on one

explanation.surface: Someone is paying off a television set in instalments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instalments' tempts you toward hire purchase; the question mark signals the other sense, parts of a broadcast serial.
explanation.definitionFit: A serial programme is broadcast in parts, each one a single instalment of the story.

clue.text: An alcoholic drink leads to a complaint

parts.note: gin is a spirit, an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Drinking spirits leads to a medical complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' is only a link joining the drink to the second A.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can be an illness or ailment; this one is chest pain from poor blood supply to the heart.

explanation.surface: Orders are issued to troops under arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arms' is heraldry: the devices on a coat of arms are its armorial bearings.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass heading is a direction; a charge displayed on a heraldic shield is also so called.

explanation.surface: Someone forgets to drop something off.
explanation.definitionFit: To forget to include something, or to exclude it on purpose, is to skip it.

parts.note: reads as a remark on rare love, but points to love that is not returned, a kind not shared in common by both

explanation.surface: A wistful remark that true love is rare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'common' means shared by two people: love that only one side feels is not common to both.
explanation.definitionFit: Love that is not returned by its object is one-sided, felt by just one party.

clue.text: It shows distance covered in playing extra time

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of extra time are toyed with and rearranged

explanation.surface: A football match goes into extra time, and something records how far the players ran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges EXTRA TIME; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab's meter records the distance travelled and calculates the fare.

clue.text: Refuse to fold over the sheet

explanation.surface: Someone declines to make the bed properly.
explanation.definitionFit: To reject an offer is to refuse it; folding back the top sheet of a made bed is the hotel ritual of the same name.

clue.text: Those taking part in the arms race?

definitions.text: Those taking part in the arms race?

parts.words: Those taking part in the arms race?
parts.note: the arms race usually means nations building weapons; here it is read as people racing to move weapons illegally

explanation.surface: A comment on the nations competing in a weapons build-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arms race' wants to be the Cold War stockpiling; the question mark recasts it as smugglers running weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Smugglers who carry weapons illegally across borders are traffickers in arms.

indicators.note: into a spin means the letters of ray gets whirl around into a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Ray panics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into a spin' rearranges RAY GETS, and the whole clue also describes the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone going into a spin is whirling round, turning on the spot.

parts.note: revolver suggests a handgun, but means anything that rotates, whose pin is the line it turns around

explanation.surface: A question about a part of a handgun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolver' looks like a gun; here it is anything that revolves, like a wheel or a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating body turns about a central line or spindle, the pivot of its spin.

clue.text: Do crossword books prove financially viable?

parts.note: to do a crossword is to solve it
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Asking whether publishing puzzle books can make money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prove' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A business with assets exceeding its debts can pay its way and is financially viable.

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of we sold are put out of order

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper says the stock of pegs has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges WE SOLD; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooden pins used to join pieces of furniture are pegs.

clue.text: Telephoned about religious instruction, being enthusiastic

indicators.note: about means the word for telephoned goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: rang means telephoned
RI is the abbreviation for religious instruction, a school subject

explanation.surface: Someone phoned about scripture lessons, keen as ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts RANG around RI; 'being' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone eager and impatient to start is keen and enthusiastic.

clue.text: Two kings embracing are not seen so often

indicators.note: embracing means the two abbreviations hold the word are between them

parts.note: R, for rex, is the abbreviation for king; two of them give RR

explanation.surface: Two monarchs embracing is an unusual sight.
explanation.walkthrough: R is from Latin rex, king; 'embracing' puts ARE between the two Rs.
explanation.definitionFit: Something less common, occurring less frequently, is seen less often.

clue.text: A learner gets behind in class, being casual

indicators.note: gets behind means the learner's letters follow the phrase for in class

parts.note: in form means in class, a form being a school class in Britain
L is the abbreviation for learner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: A pupil falls behind in lessons and is too relaxed about it.
explanation.walkthrough: A FORM is a school class in Britain; 'gets behind' places A and L after IN FORM.
explanation.definitionFit: Relaxed, without ceremony or formality, means casual.

indicators.note: not tells you to remove the letters meaning in favour from the objection

parts.note: a protest is an objection
pro means in favour of

explanation.surface: A complaint against an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes PRO from PROTEST; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An examination or trial of knowledge is a test.

explanation.surface: A company's dealings go into decline.
explanation.definitionFit: A company's total sales are its business volume; and to flip something upside down is to reverse it.

explanation.surface: Someone decides to stop travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is to come to rest and stay put, as settlers do, rather than continue on.
explanation.definitionFit: To resolve a matter is to decide it; to make one's home in a place rather than keep travelling is to stop moving on.

clue.text: Calm sentry that is becoming agitated

indicators.note: becoming agitated means the letters are stirred up and rearranged

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A guard who was composed grows nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming agitated' rearranges SENTRY plus IE.
explanation.definitionFit: A state of peaceful composure, free from disturbance, is calm as a noun.

indicators.note: turbulent suggests disorder, so the letters of priest are thrown about

explanation.surface: A rebellious cleric has a sharp sense of humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a turbulent priest' echoes Henry II on Thomas Becket; 'turbulent' rearranges PRIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively cleverness and sparkle of mind, borrowed from French, is wit.
